Eggs of the zebrafish Danio rerio measure approximately 0.07 cm  in diameter, a size consistent with the small, transparent, and demersal eggs typical of cyprinids. The yolk itself represents a substantial portion of this volume, with reported yolk diameters ranging from 0.055 to 0.075 cm, though the protective chorion brings the overall egg diameter to about 0.09 cm. Each fertilised ovum contains a modest endowment of organic material, with a recorded egg dry weight of 0.0001 grams , a value that constrains the duration of the endotrophic larval phase. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a clear developmental schedule emerges: hatching occurs after roughly 5 days [ab = roughly 5 days], yielding a prolarva that still retains a prominent yolk sac. At this stage of emergence, the newly hatched alevin measures 0.4 cm [Lb = 0.4 cm] in total length at birth, still reliant on endogenous reserves. The swim bladder inflates shortly thereafter, marking the onset of active feeding and the transition to an exogenously feeding, free-swimming larva. This embryonic and early larval trajectory is highly temperature-dependent, and the 5-day incubation period observed at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] shortens appreciably under warmer regimes. Under standard laboratory conditions at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], females consistently exhibited a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of approximately 15% [GSI = approximately 15%].

The larval period is punctuated by a metamorphic transformation that reorganises the body plan and initiates the juvenile phenotype. Metamorphosis typically occurs at a total length of 1 cm , at which point the adult fin ray pattern and pigmentation become fully established. Under a thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], this morphological transformation is achieved 22 days  after hatching, representing a critical developmental milestone. The post-metamorphic juvenile, now fully exotrophic, embarks on a rapid somatic growth phase that ultimately leads to sexual maturation. Puberty, defined by the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females and active spermatogenesis in males, is attained at a total length of approximately 3.25 cm [Lp = approximately 3.25 cm]; this value integrates the standard length measured at first egg laying in females, which ranges from 2.4 to 2.6 cm standard length, with a conversion factor reflecting the proportional contribution of the caudal fin to total length. The onset of first reproduction in Danio rerio occurs at 75 days after hatching [tR = 75 days after hatching] when maintained at a mean temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], though individual variation spanning 74 to 75 days of development has been documented. This relatively early maturation, combined with continuous, group-synchronous oocyte development, underpins the species' high fecundity and its utility as a laboratory model.

Under optimal captive conditions, adult zebrafish achieve a maximum recorded total length of 5 cm [Li = 5 cm], a modest asymptotic size that is typical of small-bodied cyprinids. The corresponding adult wet mass plateaus at an ultimate wet weight of 1 gram [Wwi = 1 gram], a value that reflects the streamlined, fusiform body plan adapted for mid-water foraging. Longevity data from laboratory populations indicate that the oldest documented individuals reach a lifespan of approximately 4.5 years [am = approximately 4.5 years] when maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a relatively extended duration for a fish of this diminutive size. Reproductive output rises in tandem with body size and nutritional condition. At 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a fully mature female can produce 240 eggs per day [Ri = 240 eggs per day], a rate that underscores the species' high reproductive turnover and its capacity for rapid population growth under favourable conditions. The daily egg deposition rate represents a substantial energetic outflow, and females must maintain elevated ingestion rates to sustain this level of gamete production.

Comparative studies within the Danio genus highlight several life-history traits that distinguish D. rerio from its congeners. For instance, the egg diameter of about 0.07 cm  and the egg dry weight of 0.0001 grams  are intermediate among cyprinids, reflecting a trade-off between fecundity and per-offspring investment. Species such as Danio aequipinnatus produce slightly larger eggs, while others produce more numerous but smaller ova. The total length at birth of 0.4 cm [Lb = 0.4 cm] aligns with the general pattern among small-bodied danionins of producing highly altricial, yolk-dependent prolarvae that complete their yolk absorption within the first few days of exogenous feeding. The rapid metamorphosis to the juvenile form at 1 cm  and the relatively short interval to first reproduction at 75 days post-hatching [tR = 75 days post-hatching] both point to a life-history strategy that prioritises early maturation and high fecundity over extended somatic growth at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. Adults attain a maximum total length of 5 cm [Li = 5 cm], and the asymptotic body mass reaches 1 gram [Wwi = 1 gram] — values consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by this schedule, as maximal body size is attained before reproductive output peaks. These demographic parameters collectively contribute to the species' classification as an opportunistic strategist.

The physiological underpinnings of the zebrafish's developmental tempo are closely tied to ambient temperature, which modulates the rates of embryogenesis, larval growth, and gonadal maturation. Under the standard laboratory temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the age at birth of 5 days [ab = 5 days] and the age at metamorphosis of 22 days  define a compressed developmental window that quickly yields a feeding, free-swimming juvenile. Once the juvenile stage is reached, the trajectory toward first reproduction at 75 days from hatching [tR = 75 days from hatching] proceeds at a pace that is regulated by temperature and food availability at a temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. The maximum lifespan of 4.5 years [am = 4.5 years] at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] is considerably shorter than that of larger, slower-maturing cyprinids, yet it encompasses numerous spawning cycles. Females can release 240 eggs per day [Ri = 240 eggs per day] during peak reproductive activity, when the gonadosomatic index was 15% [GSI = 15%] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The combination of small body size, rapid development, and prolific reproduction makes Danio rerio a model organism for studies of developmental plasticity and life-history evolution under varying thermal and nutritional environments.
